profile: Opens a paragraph by picking up the last one's point, often as a conditional or a restated claim: 'If the signs are present and plain and yet we still pass them by, the fault is on our side.' / 'Placing the fault in the receiver has two consequences.'
Ends a paragraph on the point itself, often a short flat sentence rather than a flourish: 'In most of us, it is not working.' / 'Most of us see only the lamp.'
Short to medium declarative sentences, many under fifteen words; 'and' joins two items or clauses but rarely chains three: 'It is not easy and it requires a great deal of training.'

Semicolons set two halves against each other; 'whereas' and colons are used sparingly for contrast and lists: 'God is not withholding signs; we are failing to receive them.' / 'Eyes and ears take in the surface of things, whereas inside a human being there should be something more'

Brings a verse in with a short sentence that says what it will show, then explains it right after: 'The Qur'an describes the gap in one verse.' ... 'Cattle see and hear perfectly well, so the comparison cannot be about the senses.'

Names a scholar once, with a precise verb, and then lets the point carry on: 'ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi explains what passing by a sign means'; 'Imam Khomeini insists'; 'Mohammad Ali Shomali makes the same point'

The lecturer is 'Sheikh Bahmanpour' on first mention, then 'the Sheikh', with 'in the Sheikh's words' rather than repeated 'he says': 'it is, in the Sheikh's words, a path that "has a beginning and no end"'
Inclusive 'we'/'us' and the occasional 'let's'; 'you' almost never outside the front matter; never scolds: 'We have heard these verses many times and we accept that there are signs in them'
Plain, concrete diction with everyday images: 'a person who sees a red light thinks of the danger it warns of, not of the colour and shape of the lamp'; 'There is a machine inside which is [rusted]'
Glosses Arabic terms in place, briefly: 'Praying, fasting and paying what is due, the wajibat'

Never uses rhetorical questions, jokes, grand abstractions, suspense or a moral at the paragraph's end; chapter openings state their subject directly: 'That something and why it is worth developing, is the subject of this chapter.'

tells: Short declarative steps that each move the argument on ('It does not leave the body completely; if it did, we would be dead.'); verse brought in with a plain sentence and explained right after, scholar named once with 'explains'.

'The great teachers of the Shia tradition make closely related points, each in his own words' is a vague, wordy opener; Author A would name the scholar and the point at once ('ʿAllama Tabatabaʾi tells the traveller...')

Quotation follows quotation ('...pleasure and his worship is not for the sake of God'. It is his own self that he worships, 'though he may not admit it...') with no explanation; Author A explains a quotation in plain words afterwards
The paragraph ends on a bare quotation ('his efforts are rendered invalid'); Author A stops on a sentence of his own that makes the point
Opens by picking up the previous point ('Pursuing ʿirfan means training the soul'), glosses shirk briefly in place and stops on the point; a single attribution to the Sheikh.
'These words, he says, ... He asks why ... Telling ordinary believers to say them, he says' uses the teacher three times in four sentences as filler; Author A names him once and states the point
'The prayers themselves speak from need, as a pupil would' is only loosely linked to the Sheikh's difficulty; Author A would make the link explicit
'The servant stands there because of need and the prayer gives no other reason for coming' restates the quotation it follows instead of moving on
Concrete example first ('a particular height, voice and face'), then the term glossed; the second paragraph picks up 'the other two' and each sentence makes one step, as in the red-light passage.
'The ʿurafaʾ, he writes, consider it "..." and he recalls Imam ʿAli (as) saying that...' stacks a quotation and a second report in one 'and' chain; Author A would split them and explain each
'The scholars differ in emphasis but agree that powers are not the aim' is a summary that restates; Author A does not stop to sum up
'Mutahhari also explains why seeking them would be shirk: the goal has become something other than God' repeats what the quotation already said

Picks up 'acquired knowledge', glosses ʿaql in place, uses concrete attributes ('brown or square or useful') and moves to God with a conditional step ('If this is true of the things around us...'), as Author A does.
Picks up 'the second kind' and glosses the term in place; slight drift into the anxiety example and two attributions ('in the Sheikh's account', 'the Sheikh notes') keep this near the middle.
'he says', 'In his account', 'the Sheikh adds' gives three attributions in one paragraph; Author A names the Sheikh once and states the answer
'We have been honoured, because we are allowed to recite them' is an add-on remark that doesn't move the argument on; Author A would go straight to the invitation and its answer

Single attribution, then a plain explanation of the verse after it ('Most of us fear Allah's punishment. The people of this verse fear Him with a fear that is not about punishment at all.'), in Author A's short contrasting sentences.

Chapter opening built like the reference's: identifies the prayer, glosses it briefly, links to the earlier argument and states the chapter's subject plainly ('This chapter sets out what those prayers ask for.').

'If the faculty can be repaired, there should be people in whom it already works' picks up the last point exactly as Author A does; the verse is followed by a concrete explanation ('a name means little to a person who does not know whom it names').
'the Sheikh says ... he says ... the Sheikh says' uses the teacher three times as filler; Author A names him once
'His knowledge and bounty are all there' restates 'There is no hindrance on His side' without moving on
'Chapter One reached the same conclusion by another road, when it placed the fault in the receiver' is a tidy closing cross-reference; Author A stops on the point itself

Picks up 'that shaping', concrete image of the face, Imam Khomeini named once with 'describes'; the stacked colon plus quotation ('fixes that form: "in whichever state..."') is a small mark against it.
Each state is glossed in place, the verse is followed by a plain explanation ('That God swears by this self shows its worth.') and sentences stay short and on the point.
Paragraphs open on chained conditionals that carry the last point forward ('If deeds give the soul its form, the self ... is not fixed either'); verse explained right after; concrete worry examples.

Opens like the reference ('These words come from the Munajat Shaʿbaniyyah'), with a concrete graveside image and a plain statement of the chapter's steps; 'How deep the soul goes therefore matters' is a slightly loose link.
'It is this good life that the mystics seek' is a tidy closing line; Author A would stop on the description itself
'For the muqarrabun, the terms are entirely different from those of ordinary believers' is left as a vague, grand remark after the verse; Author A explains what the verse says in concrete terms
The peace verse is introduced and then not explained, which breaks Author A's habit of glossing each verse
